Sure! Let’s break it down into two common scenarios: | Goal | What you’ll need | Typical workflow | |------|------------------|------------------| | **Capture the *visible* portion of the current Chrome tab** (i.e., what the user actually sees on their screen) | • `pyautogui` (or `mss`)
• Optional: `pygetwindow` to locate the Chrome window | 1️⃣ Find the Chrome window’s position & size.
2️⃣ Grab a screenshot of that rectangle.
3️⃣ Save or process the image. | | **Capture a *specific* page (or the same page that’s already open)** – useful when you don’t care about the exact UI layout but just the rendered DOM | • `selenium` + `chromedriver` (or `undetected-chromedriver` if you’re dealing with anti‑bot measures)
• Optional: `pyppeteer`/`playwright` for headless browsers | 1️⃣ Launch Chrome via Selenium.
2️⃣ Navigate to the desired URL (you can pass the URL that’s currently open).
3️⃣ Call `driver.save_screenshot()` or `driver.get_screenshot_as_png()`. | --- ### 1️⃣ Screenshot the *currently visible* Chrome tab #### Prerequisites ```bash pip install pyautogui pygetwindow pillow ``` > **Tip:** On macOS you’ll need to grant “Screen Recording” permissions to your terminal / IDE. #### Code example (cross‑platform) ```python import pyautogui import pygetwindow as gw from PIL import Image def screenshot_chrome_window(output_path="chrome_screenshot.png"): # Find all Chrome windows chrome_windows = [w for w in gw.getAllTitles() if "Chrome" in w] if not chrome_windows: raise RuntimeError("No Chrome window found") # Pick the first one (or iterate over all) win_title = chrome_windows[0] win = gw.getWindowsWithTitle(win_title)[0] # Get window geometry left, top, width, height = win.left, win.top, win.width, win.height # Capture that region img = pyautogui.screenshot(region=(left, top, width, height)) img.save(output_path) print(f"Saved screenshot to {output_path}") if __name__ == "__main__": screenshot_chrome_window() ``` **What it does** 1. Finds the first Chrome window that’s currently open. 2. Uses its `left`, `top`, `width`, `height` attributes to define the region. 3. Calls `pyautogui.screenshot(region=…)` to grab that rectangle. If you want to capture *all* Chrome windows, just loop over `gw.getWindowsWithTitle(...)`. --- ### 2️⃣ Screenshot a page via Selenium (headless or visible) #### Prerequisites ```bash pip install selenium webdriver-manager ``` > **Why `webdriver-manager`?** It automatically downloads the correct ChromeDriver binary for your Chrome version, saving you the hassle of manual driver management. #### Code example (headless) ```python from selenium import webdriver from selenium.webdriver.chrome.service import Service from webdriver_manager.chrome import ChromeDriverManager from selenium.webdriver.chrome.options import Options import os def screenshot_url(url, output_path="page_screenshot.png", full_page=False): chrome_options = Options() chrome_options.add_argument("--headless") # Run without GUI chrome_options.add_argument("--disable-gpu") chrome_options.add_argument("--no-sandbox") chrome_options.add_argument("--window-size=1920,1080") # Set viewport size service = Service(ChromeDriverManager().install()) driver = webdriver.Chrome(service=service, options=chrome_options) try: driver.get(url) if full_page: # Scroll to bottom to ensure lazy‑loaded elements load driver.execute_script("window.scrollTo(0, document.body.scrollHeight);") # Take screenshot driver.save_screenshot(output_path) print(f"Screenshot saved to {output_path}") finally: driver.quit() if __name__ == "__main__": # Example usage: capture the current page that the user has open # You can replace this with any URL you want screenshot_url("https://www.example.com", full_page=True) ``` **What it does** 1. Instantiates a headless Chrome instance. 2. Navigates to the target URL. 3. Optionally scrolls to the bottom to trigger lazy loading. 4. Saves a PNG of the viewport (or full page if you set `full_page=True`). > **Full‑page screenshot**: Selenium itself doesn’t support full‑page screenshots out of the box. If you need the entire scrollable page, you can either use `driver.get_screenshot_as_base64()` after scrolling in steps, or switch to a tool like `pyppeteer`/`playwright` that supports full‑page captures natively. --- ### 3️⃣ Using Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) – a lightweight alternative If you already have Chrome running with remote debugging enabled (`chrome.exe --remote-debugging-port=9222`), you can connect to it and issue a screenshot command. #### Prerequisites ```bash pip install pychrome ``` #### Code example ```python import pychrome import base64 def screenshot_cdp(tab_id=None, output_path="cdp_screenshot.png"): browser = pychrome.Browser(url="http://127.0.0.1:9222") tabs = browser.list_tab() if not tabs: raise RuntimeError("No Chrome tabs available") # Pick the first tab if none specified tab = next((t for t in tabs if t.id == tab_id), tabs[0]) # Enable Page domain tab.start() tab.Page.enable() # Capture screenshot result = tab.Page.captureScreenshot(format="png") img_bytes = base64.b64decode(result["data"]) with open(output_path, "wb") as f: f.write(img_bytes) print(f"Screenshot saved to {output_path}") tab.stop() if __name__ == "__main__": screenshot_cdp() ``` **How to enable remote debugging** On Windows: ```cmd "C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe" --remote-debugging-port=9222 ``` On macOS/Linux: ```bash google-chrome --remote-debugging-port=9222 ``` Once Chrome is launched with that flag, the script above will connect to the existing tab and capture a screenshot. --- ## Quick Decision Flow 1. **Do you want the exact pixels that the user sees?** → Use **pyautogui** + **pygetwindow**. 2. **Do you just need a screenshot of a known URL (regardless of the user’s view)?** → Use **Selenium** (or **Playwright/pyppeteer**). 3. **Do you already have Chrome running with remote debugging?** → Use **pychrome** (CDP).
